storylets.speaker: Nereus
storylets.title: A diver's catechism.
pages: Nereus, it emerges, was a salvage diver for eleven years before the paper claimed him, and when he hears you have been down in the green dark he subjects you to the old crews' catechism: what did the cold do at the second layer, did you exhale on the way up, did you look BEHIND the wreck, never just inside, always behind, because the sea files things behind.

You pass, apparently. He produces, from the organized catastrophe of his table, a diver's slate worn smooth at the edges. 'Mine,' he says. 'From the working years. The sea and I had an arrangement: I stopped taking things that were resting, and it stopped showing me things I couldn't put down.' He does not give you the slate. He shows it to you, which from Nereus is the greater intimacy, and on it, in grease pencil faded to a ghost: a tally of dives, stopped mid-stroke at four hundred and one.

storylets.speaker: Nereus
storylets.title: The town assembles.
pages: With four pages on the table, the Almanac has begun to do the thing Nereus promised: cohere. He has them laid out in his own ordering, market notice beside harbor log beside a child's school exercise, and he walks you through Maren's Hollow as if walking you down its high street.

'Here, the chandler's quarter, they argued about paint. Here, the school, the children kept a tide journal, look at the handwriting wobble, that's a six-year-old recording a neap tide with TOTAL professional rigor.' His ink-stained finger hovers, never touching. 'People think drowned towns are tragedies. They were towns first, Tideborn. Long first. The tragedy is one night. The town is ten thousand mornings, and the sea, for reasons you and I are circling, has decided the mornings deserve the better postage.'

storylets.speaker: Nereus
storylets.title: Four hundred and two.
pages: You find him not at his table but at the end of the quay, in a borrowed drysuit nineteen years out of fashion, staring at the water with his old slate in his hand. The tally on it, you remember, stops at four hundred and one.

'Dive four hundred and one,' he says, not turning, 'was the Squall year. A schooner on the Chop. I went down for her strongbox and found her crew still at their stations, and the sea showed me, with great patience, that they were RESTING, and that I had become a man who took things from people who were resting.' The water slaps the pilings. 'I surfaced, sold my gear, and bought a loupe. Eleven years of paper. Safe as houses, paper. It only ever shows you the mornings.'

He weighs the slate, and then, with the suddenness of a man jumping before the cold can argue, he hands it to you and starts down the ladder. 'The Almanac says there are pages in the shallow wrecks that wax won't have saved much longer. Number four hundred and two, Tideborn. Mark it for me. And mind the second layer; the cold's a liar there.'

storylets.speaker: Nereus
storylets.title: Archive hours.
pages: Nereus is deep in a page and acknowledges you with one raised tweezer, which in his sign language means: sit, be silent or be useful. You sort wax fragments by curvature for half an hour while he mutters dates, and when you leave he says, with feeling, 'You have steadier hands than the gull I usually get. Come back.' It is unclear, and will remain unclear, whether the gull was a metaphor.

storylets.speaker: Nereus
storylets.title: Comparing logbooks.
pages: Nereus dives again, shallow and careful, two mornings a week, and the slate tally is climbing past four hundred and ten. He debriefs you like a fellow professional now, trading layer reports and wreck gossip, and his table holds two loupes, because he assumes, correctly, that sooner or later you will want to read the pages yourself rather than wait for the post.

storylets.speaker: Nereus
storylets.title: The dawn run, printed.
pages: Nereus has something rare on the table tonight: not handwriting, print. A ferry timetable, typeset, official, the Lantern Jane's summer schedule, salvaged whole in its wax like a fly in amber. 'Do you know how few printed pages the sea has posted?' he says. 'Nine. Nine, out of hundreds. The sea does not much care for print, Tideborn. Print is what a town says to strangers. The sea has been sending us what the town said to itself.'

But this page it kept, and when he walks you through it you see why: the margins. The neat printed grid of crossings is annotated in the quick certain scrawl until the print is nearly an afterthought, fares waived and noted, a dawn run added, a crossing held eleven minutes for a late wedding party, and beside the last sailing of the day, in the smallest writing on the page: 'Never miss this one. The lamp waits up.' Nereus rewraps it with his surgeon's tenderness. 'A schedule,' he says, 'is a promise typeset. I have read every page the sea has sent, and I tell you professionally: this town believed its boat the way other towns believe the tide tables. Take it. It should live with whoever keeps the promise now.'

storylets.speaker: Nereus
storylets.title: Greywater, living.
pages: The clean table did not stay clean, and you are relieved to see it: Nereus has a new book open, blank pages, good paper, and across the cover in his careful archivist's hand: GREYWATER, LIVING. VOLUME ONE. 'I spent twenty years reading a drowned town's mornings,' he says, 'and it taught me exactly one thing worth a book: nobody writes the mornings down while they're having them. So.' He taps the page. 'I interview the quay now. Mirabel gave me the history of the stove, which has OPINIONS, it turns out, going back three landladies. Sefton lied to me about knots for two hours, magnificently. The bait boy's war with the gulls runs to four pages and I have had to open a file.'

He dips his pen and looks at you with the sudden total attention of the heron he has always been. 'Entry the first, though, I saved. Sit down, captain. Start where you like. The shingle, the key, the first tide out, I'll keep up.' And you realize, as the pen starts to move, that the sea kept its records of you for nineteen years, and now the land intends to keep its own, and between the two ledgers you are, for the first time in either life, thoroughly written down.
